title: Voxel Network Lab is now Tulip Labs
body: Same lab, same tracks, same progress in your browser, with a new name to match the pixel tulip. Tulip Labs is a product by svx.
more: The lab started as a handful of voxel worlds, and the old name described exactly that. It has since grown into seven tracks, from DSA to building your own database, and the name no longer fit.
We picked the tulip because of how learning works here. Every chapter you finish grows a flower in your garden, a block at a time. The pixel tulip was already our logo, so the name followed it.
Nothing you rely on has moved. Your progress still lives in this browser, every link still works, and every chapter is still free.
list: New name: Tulip Labs, a product by svx
A TL monogram in the top bar; point at it to see the full name
Your progress, links and tracks stay exactly as they were

title: A new face, and a look inside the lab
body: The home page now shows what learning here is actually like: four real moments from the tracks, played on one stage.
more: It is hard to tell what a course feels like from a list of chapter titles. So the home page now plays four real moments from the lab: a simulation you watch and then write, a blueprint that stacks as you build, a hidden test that fails slow code, and the garden that grows as you go.
Each moment has a few chapters you can jump straight into. The track cards became small posters in each track's colour, and moving between pages now happens behind a curtain of pink pixels.
list: Four moments on one stage, each with chapters to jump into
Track cards redrawn as posters
Page changes in pink pixels, skipped if you prefer reduced motion

title: Every chapter now has a blueprint and a map
body: Each chapter shows its parts as voxel blocks that stack as you finish steps. Every course page draws a map of how its chapters wire together.
more: Before you write a line, you can now see what you are building. Every chapter opens with a blueprint: its parts drawn as voxel blocks, faint until you finish the step that builds them. Finish them all and the build is stamped as shipped.
The blueprint also says what the chapter builds on and what it leads to. On each course page, a map draws every chapter and the wires between them, so you can see the whole course at once.
list: A blueprint at the top of every chapter
Blocks stack as you finish steps
A map of the whole course on each track page

title: Data structures and algorithms, from the ground floor to Codeforces
body: Forty-four chapters from Big-O to lazy segment trees. Every pattern starts as a simulation, and every question has a big hidden test.
more: The DSA track starts at the ground floor, with what Big-O really counts, and climbs to the patterns used in contests: two pointers, sliding windows, monotonic stacks, graphs, dynamic programming and segment trees.

Every pattern starts as a simulation that counts the work as it goes, so you can see why one approach is faster. Every question then has a big hidden test, so code that is correct but slow fails, just like it would in an interview.
list: 44 chapters, from Big-O to lazy segment trees
A simulation that counts the work for every pattern
Hidden tests big enough to catch slow code

title: Light mode everywhere, and Auto that follows your laptop
body: Every page, home included, now has a warm paper light mode. Auto switches live when your laptop does.
more: The lab used to be dark only. Every page now has a light mode on warm paper, with the same colours tuned so they stay easy to read.
Pick Light, Dark or Auto from the section menu in the top bar. Auto follows your laptop and switches live, so the lab goes dark in the evening when your screen does.
list: Light, Dark and Auto on every page
Auto switches live with your system
Your choice is remembered in this browser

title: Build your own X, and Probability & Stats
body: Build a calculator, a programming language, a regex engine and a database, one real part at a time. Or simulate probability first and prove it after.
more: Build your own X takes tools you use every day and has you rebuild them from nothing, one real part per step: a calculator, a programming language, a regex engine, git, a database, and more.

Probability & Stats works the other way round from most courses. You simulate a question first, flipping a thousand coins or drawing a thousand samples, and watch the answer appear. Then you prove why it came out that way.
list: Build your own X: rebuild real tools one part at a time
Probability & Stats: simulate first, prove after

title: Real Python in your browser, with nothing to install
body: The code tracks run real Python right in the page. Each chapter climbs a ladder, and wrong answers come back later for review.
more: Every code track now runs real Python inside the page. There is nothing to install and no account to make: open a chapter and press run.

Each chapter climbs the same ladder. First you predict what some code does, then fix a bug, then put lines in order, then write it yourself, and finally rebuild it from memory. Anything you get wrong comes back later in your review queue.
list: Real Python, running in your browser
A five-step ladder in every chapter
Wrong answers come back for review

title: The lab opens with twelve 3D worlds you can poke
body: Cities, sandpiles, flocks and forest fires as voxel worlds, each with a guided story, a notebook of ideas and a quiz.
more: The lab opened with twelve worlds about complexity, built from voxels you can poke: a city that grows, a sandpile that topples, a flock that steers itself, a forest that burns and grows back.
Each world comes with a guided story that walks you through what you are seeing, a notebook of the ideas behind it, and a short quiz at the end.
list: Twelve voxel worlds
A guided story, a notebook and a quiz for each
